See original. As Influenza Cases Rise, WHO Recommends Vaccine Composition for 2027 Kesehatan 00:00 00:00 10 10 1.00x JAKARTA, KOMPAS — The World Health Organization has recommended the composition of the influenza vaccine for the southern hemisphere influenza season of 2027. This recommendation was issued amid an increase in influenza activity globally, while the situation in Indonesia as of September 2026 is categorized as moderate. In an announcement on September 25, 2026, the WHO stated that the influenza vaccine needs to be updated regularly due to the continuous changes in the virus. This recommendation serves as a reference for regulatory bodies and pharmaceutical companies in developing, producing, and granting usage permits for the vaccine for the upcoming season. The WHO recommends three virus components for the 2027 seasonal influenza vaccine in the Southern Hemisphere, namely influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and influenza B from the Victoria lineage. There has indeed been an increase in influenza cases. The recommended composition varies according to the vaccine production technology. For egg-based vaccines, the WHO recommends the A/Missouri/11/2025-like (H1N1)pdm09 virus, A/Darwin/1454/2025-like (H3N2), and B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025-like from the Victoria lineage. Meanwhile, for cell culture-based vaccines, recombinant protein, or nucleic acid, the recommended components are A/Missouri/11/2025-like (H1N1)pdm09, A/Darwin/1415/2025-like (H3N2), and B/Pennsylvania/14/2025-like from the Victoria lineage. KOMPAS/ADRYAN YOGA PARAMADWYA A doctor administers the influenza vaccine to a patient at the Aisyah Primary Clinic in Jakarta on Monday, January 5, 2026. The recommendation was formulated based on the monitoring of influenza viruses circulating in various countries. The WHO noted that from February to August 2026, the influenza viruses A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and influenza B circulated with varying proportions across different regions of the world. Influenza A virus is the most commonly found type in most regions. However, influenza B dominates in North and West Africa, North America, and East Asia. Advertisement Iklan According to WHO, the influenza season in the southern hemisphere is a period when influenza transmission tends to increase in southern hemisphere countries, generally from May to October. WHO updates the vaccine composition recommendations for that season so that the vaccine can be adjusted to the viruses expected to circulate. Although Indonesia is located in the southern hemisphere, the influenza pattern in this tropical country does not entirely follow the winter season, and an increase in cases can occur throughout the year. Read MoreHow to Prevent Infection with the Current Influenza A Pandemic? The WHO updates its vaccine composition recommendations twice a year through consultations with experts from collaboration centers and essential regulatory laboratories. They review surveillance data from the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) as well as other sources. The Director of the WHO's Epidemiology and Pandemic Management, Maria Van Kerkhove, stated that international cooperation in sharing data, viruses, and expertise enables the organization to provide timely vaccine recommendations. "For nearly 75 years, the WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System has demonstrated the strength of global solidarity in public health," said Maria. According to him, this collaboration strengthens the world's ability to detect and respond to the ever-evolving threat of influenza. H1N1 dominant in Indonesia In Indonesia, the Ministry of Health recorded an influenza positivity rate of 56 percent in the 38th week of 2026. However, influenza activity in community health center surveillance is still in the moderate category, while hospital surveillance is in the low category. Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin, in a press statement on Monday (28/9/2026), stated that the increase in influenza cases needs to be addressed by strengthening surveillance and preparedness, rather than through panic. Read MoreInfluenza A Spreads, Should We Be Worried? "There has indeed been an increase in influenza cases, particularly in Indonesia and Southeast Asia. However, based on the surveillance data we have, the situation is still within a medium range. Therefore, what we are doing is enhancing surveillance and preparedness so that the development of cases can continue to be monitored," said Budi. Advertisement Iklan Sentinel surveillance results indicate that influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 became the dominant virus in Indonesia in week 38 of 2026. Of the 265 specimens examined during that period, 148 tested positive for influenza. This resulted in a positivity rate of 56 percent. KOMPAS The cases of influenza A have been reported to be increasing in Africa, the United States, Europe, and Asia. In Indonesia, the Ministry of Health has stated that influenza A has been detected in 13 provinces. The Ministry of Health stated that the increase in influenza activity in August-September is still in line with the seasonal pattern that has been observed in Indonesia. In addition to influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, the government is also monitoring the development of influenza A(H3N2) subclade K, which has recently been widely referred to as "superflu." The Ministry of Health emphasized that the term "superflu" is not an official nomenclature used by the WHO or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to refer to subclade K. Therefore, the development of influenza needs to be assessed based on laboratory examination results and surveillance data, rather than solely on terms circulating in the community. Based on sentinel surveillance ILI-SARI, from 2025 to the 38th week of 2026, there were 188 results from subclade K examinations recorded. Of these, 166 findings originated from 2025, while the remaining 22 findings were recorded in 2026. Read MoreBeware of "Super Flu" in Children: Influenza A Subclade K Is Not the Ordinary Flu "For what is referred to as 'superflu' or H3N2 subclade K, the data we are monitoring actually shows that the number of cases this year is lower compared to last year. Therefore, we need to distinguish between the circulating information and the conditions based on surveillance data," said Budi. Monitoring is carried out through sentinel surveillance involving community health centers, hospitals, laboratories and health quarantine centers. Beware of complications The Ministry of Health reminds that the majority of influenza patients can recover with supportive care and do not require hospitalization. The use of antiviral medications, such as oseltamivir, is also not intended for all patients. Advertisement Iklan According to Budi, oseltamivir should be used appropriately and limited to patients with severe conditions or patients with comorbidities requiring antiviral treatment based on medical considerations. KOMPAS/ADRYAN YOGA PARAMADWYA Flubio influenza vaccine at the Aisyah Primary Clinic, Jakarta, Monday (January 5, 2026). The restriction on the use of antivirals is necessary to prevent the emergence of resistance. If the virus becomes resistant to the medication, treatment options may become increasingly limited during more severe outbreaks. "We must not use antivirals excessively because there is a risk of resistance. If resistance occurs, we could lose treatment options when facing more severe and life-threatening outbreaks, such as H5Nx influenza," said Budi. In addition to monitoring the viruses circulating among humans, the WHO is also examining the influenza viruses that are present in animals, particularly those that have caused infections in humans. Read MoreInfluenza Vaccine Effective in Preventing Severe Infections Caused by Superflu The zoonotic influenza virus remains a concern due to its potential to trigger a pandemic. During biannual consultations, experts also select candidates for new vaccine viruses that can be used to expedite vaccine production in the event of a pandemic threat. In Indonesia, the Ministry of Health continues to strengthen influenza surveillance, the readiness of healthcare facilities and laboratories, as well as risk communication to the public. The public is urged to adopt clean and healthy living behaviors, wear masks when ill or in crowded places, and practice cough and sneeze etiquette. Medical examinations need to be conducted if symptoms worsen. Special attention is also required for vulnerable groups, such as infants and young children, the elderly, pregnant women, and individuals with underlying health conditions, who are at a higher risk of experiencing influenza complications. JAKARTA, KOMPAS — The World Health Organization has recommended the composition of the influenza vaccine for the southern hemisphere influenza season of 2027. This recommendation was issued amid an increase in influenza activity globally, while the situation in Indonesia as of September 2026 is categorized as moderate. In an announcement on September 25, 2026, the WHO stated that the influenza vaccine needs to be updated regularly due to the continuous changes in the virus. This recommendation serves as a reference for regulatory bodies and pharmaceutical companies in developing, producing, and granting usage permits for the vaccine for the upcoming season. The WHO recommends three virus components for the 2027 seasonal influenza vaccine in the Southern Hemisphere, namely influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and influenza B from the Victoria lineage. supplementary_news.content_title: Flu season approaches with more vaccine choices this year. Here’s what CT experts are saying
supplementary_news.content: FILE – A certified medical assistant holds a syringe for a flu vaccine at a clinic in Seattle, on Sept. 10, 2025. (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson, File) By Stephen Underwood | sunderwood@courant.com | Hartford Courant PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 6:00 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Autumn marks the beginning of the annual flu season, when more people begin to congregate indoors and viruses spread faster. But this year, new vaccine options are available, and doctors are urging nearly everyone to get vaccinated. While flu levels currently remain low across Connecticut, health care officials said they are expecting numbers to spike during the holiday season as more people congregate indoors. The beginning of school is also a big component for viral spread, as more people congregate in confined spaces. Influenza, or more commonly known as the flu, is a potentially serious disease that can lead to hospitalization and sometimes even death, according to the Centers for Disease Control . Everyone 6 months and older in the United States, with rare exception, should get a flu vaccine every season, CDC officials said. Flu vaccinations have been shown to have many benefits, including reducing the risk of flu illnesses, hospitalizations and even the risk of flu-related death. “We don’t know what the big strains will be yet until they show up and we can confirm a match,” said Dr. Ulysses Wu , chief epidemiologist with Hartford HealthCare . “But I would suspect it’s going to be similar to last year. There are two ways you can view the flu season, the flu itself will circulate probably very similar to last year. However, the human response to it may make it a busier season if people are not getting the vaccines.” According to the CDC, all flu vaccines for the upcoming season will be trivalent. This means they are formulated to protect against three main seasonal influenza Type A and B viruses: an A(H1N1) virus, an A(H3N2) virus, and a B/Victoria lineage virus. “The purpose of the vaccine is not necessarily to protect you from getting the flu, but to keep you out of the hospital and keep you from getting really sick,” Wu said. “Even last year when we saw there was a little mismatch of strains, it still modulates your immune response that you’re still able to put up a fight. If you look back to COVID, we had not seen anything like that before, so our immune systems were not able to fight it as well. But now with vaccinations and with people getting COVID, now our immune system is ready. That’s similar to what the flu vaccine will do. Its main job is to keep you out of the hospital and from dying.” Wu said that peak flu months usually occur around end of January, February and March. But he noted that each year peak season has been arriving earlier Last year, according to Wu, flu season ran through April before cases started to dwindle by May. Some meteorologists are predicting a more mild early winter season due to the effects of El Nino, which could have an impact on this year’s flu season, Wu said. If the weather is more mild, people may congregate less indoors. However, the holiday season tends to see a spike each year as people congregate for parties, celebrations and gatherings. “Everyone should get the flu vaccine, it’s safe and effective,” Wu said. “Sometimes I hear people say ‘I got the flu from the flu shot’ which is absolutely impossible. What they are experiencing is an immune response from the shot. That is actually a good thing because it means the immune system is working, which is demonstrating the effectiveness of the vaccine.” Wu said that people should begin getting the flu shot anytime after Halloween to ensure long-lasting immunity that will last through the end of flu season in April. Immunity from flu vaccination is generally thought to last for around four to six months before losing some efficacy, according to the CDC. While some may want to get the flu vaccine earlier, Wu said Nov. 1 is generally considered when people should begin getting vaccinated. This year, Americans have more options available for flu vaccines than in prior years. A new option this season is mFLUSIVA, the first FDA-approved mRNA flu vaccine injection, according to Wu. It is approved for adults 50 to 64 years old and received accelerated approval for adults 65 and older. It is the first FDA-approved mRNA-based influenza vaccine injection. Unlike traditional egg-based or cell-based vaccines that use inactive or weakened virus particles, mFLUSIVA delivers genetic instructions telling cells to temporarily produce harmless copies of proteins, which the immune system then begins building targeted antibodies for, according to the CDC. Because mRNA technology bypasses the slow process of growing viruses in eggs, mRNA manufacturing allows for later influenza strain selection and fast production, unlike traditional vaccines. The hope is that the mRNA vaccine can target emerging strains quicker, according to the CDC. FluMist is also another option, which instead of injection form, is a live influenza vaccine nasal spray for people ages 2 to 49 years old and contains egg proteins. It may not be recommended during pregnancy or for people who are immunocompromised or have certain medical conditions. FluMist uses a live, but weakened, virus, the CDC said. The nasal spray cannot replicate or cause full-blown influenza in healthy people, but a mild immune response is common. “All of the flu vaccines are safe and effective,” Wu said. “It really just depends on the method of delivery you choose. The new mRNA vaccine has shown very good promise with bolstering immune response. That vaccine is recommended for those over 50 years old. The flu nasal spray is usually for children, since it does not require injection, but kids with asthma or anyone who is immune-compromised should not get that one, as it is a weakened but live virus. If anyone has questions about which one to get, they should talk with their doctor.” During last year’s influenza season, the Connecticut Department of Public Health reported a year-end total of 190 flu-associated deaths for the season, according to state health data. In addition, there were 41,000 reported cases, with nearly 3,700 hospitalizations. The vast majority of hospitalizations and deaths occurred among the elderly. Wu said that young people should also get vaccinated, as it can help reduce the spread to more vulnerable populations. “The main point is that vaccines work and they are safe,” Wu said. “Each year, tens of thousands of people die from the flu. It is a deadly virus for some. The good news is many deaths are preventable because of vaccines. We recommend nearly everyone, except those with severe allergic reactions to the vaccine, to get vaccinated. Vaccines not only can save your life, but they can save someone you love as well.” Stephen Underwood can be reached at sunderwood@courant.com. supplementary_news.content: TEMPO EXCLUSIVE Tempo English Support Tempo LOGIN REGISTER Home Popular News News Asean & Beyond Sport Environment Sci & Tech Life & Style Outreach Interviews Photo Index Horizons & People Opinion Your View & Story World Home National Deputy Health Minister: Influenza A Usually Resolves on Its Own Reporter Antara September 30, 2026 | 04:43 pm Share Article link copied A health worker displays the Flubio influenza vaccine at the Aisyah Primary Clinic, Taman Sari, Jakarta, January 5, 2026. Health experts emphasize the importance of double vaccination and a healthy lifestyle as the primary defenses to prevent economic disruption due to high worker absenteeism. The superflu phenomenon serves as a reminder for the world to continue adapting to the rapid mutation of respiratory viruses. Antara/Sulthony Hasanuddin TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Indonesia’s Deputy Health Minister Dante Saksono Herbuwono said most influenza A infections are generally mild and can resolve on their own, although the government continues to monitor case numbers and severity. “This is a self-limiting disease, a disease that heals by itself without treatment. So influenza A is not dangerous,” Dante said at a press conference at the Government Communication Agency (Bakom RI) office in Jakarta on Wednesday. Dante said current monitoring showed no significant increase in influenza cases, either nationally or globally. He said the spread of influenza A follows a pattern similar to seasonal influenza, with cases tending to increase ahead of Indonesia’s rainy season before declining in February and March. Regarding information about influenza A, Dante urged the public to respond proportionally and avoid unnecessary alarm. “Don’t hype this up and turn it into viral news, making it seem frightening. It’s not frightening at all. Influenza A is just like regular influenza,” he said. Influenza A is a type of influenza caused by influenza A viruses and can spread through respiratory droplets. Symptoms can include fever, cough, sore throat, muscle aches, headaches and fatigue. The Health Ministry monitors influenza through surveillance at 39 community health centers, 35 hospitals and 14 health quarantine offices. According to reports through week 38, influenza activity was classified as moderate. Health Ministry surveillance data also showed that the influenza positivity rate reached 56 percent in week 38. The dominant strain currently circulating in Indonesia is influenza A(H1N1)pdm09. Several provinces recorded relatively high proportions of positive influenza cases, including Southeast Sulawesi at 37 percent, Jakarta at 31 percent and the Bangka Belitung Islands at 29 percent. While most people with influenza recover without special treatment, the World Health Organization (WHO) says influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among high-risk groups such as young children, older adults, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions. supplementary_news.content: メインコンテンツへスキップ Why does influenza spread early in Okinawa? A thorough explanation of 5 factors and the much-discussed 'Subclade K' こむぎのつぶやき 2026年10月1日 16:45 The 2026–2027 influenza season recorded a nationwide epidemic in late August (week 34), the second earliest since statistics began. As the number of infections surges across the country, Okinawa Prefecture has reached 26.27 cases per sentinel site, and Tokyo has reached 15.21 cases, reaching extremely high infection levels. While influenza is strongly associated with winter, why does it spread in Okinawa from summer to autumn, ahead of the rest of the country? We will explain in an easy-to-understand manner the 5 factors behind this, the true nature of the variant Subclade K that has been causing global concern in recent years, and the latest vaccine situation. 5 factors behind the early influenza epidemic in Okinawa 1. Formation of artificial 'enclosed and dry' spaces due to air conditioning Because Okinawa experiences intense heat and humidity from summer to autumn, strong air conditioning is used daily in schools, workplaces, homes, and commercial facilities. Lack of ventilation: Air stagnates because windows are kept closed for long periods. Indoor dryness: Indoor humidity drops due to air conditioning and dehumidification functions. Contrary to the humidity outdoors, a major cause is that an 'enclosed, dry environment prone to droplet infection similar to winter' is artificially created indoors. Furthermore, research has shown that 'frequent ventilation' is highly effective in infection control. 2. Active tourism and human movement from within and outside the country Okinawa is one of the country's leading tourist destinations, and it receives many inbound travelers from overseas, including Asian countries. Virus introduction from the Southern Hemisphere: It is an environment where strains that have spread in the Southern Hemisphere, which has the opposite season to Japan, are easily introduced. Introduction from tropical regions: Due to the flow of people from tropical regions such as Southeast Asia, where the virus is prevalent year-round, the virus enters early. 3. Subtropical climate and the 'summer-over' phenomenon In tropical and subtropical regions such as Southeast Asia, it is common for the virus to spread multiple times a year (year-round type), rather than being concentrated in winter. Impact of rainy season and rainfall: During periods of heavy rain, indoor activities increase, ventilation becomes insufficient, and infections spread more easily. Virus circulation (summer-over): Even in Okinawa, which belongs to the subtropics, the virus continues to circulate through the summer (summer-over phenomenon) and expands without waiting for the full-scale winter. 4. Intense community interaction and school/household composition Summer to autumn is a time when opportunities for group contact, especially among the younger generation, increase rapidly. Group activities: Infections spread easily due to club activity expeditions and training camps during summer vacation, classroom life after school resumes, and Obon or local festivals. Multi-generational transmission: Okinawa has a higher proportion of children compared to the mainland, creating an environment where household infections starting from children and transmission to the elderly are likely to occur. In fact, about 85% of cluster infection cases occur in nursery schools and elementary schools. 5. Decline in physical strength and immunity due to summer fatigue and air conditioning Due to factors such as sleep deprivation and summer fatigue caused by severe heat, and autonomic nervous system disruption from the temperature difference between indoors and outdoors, this is a period when an individual's basic immune function is prone to decline, which also encourages the spread. What are this season's prevalent strain and the much-discussed mutant 'Subclade K'? Currently, the 'A(H1N1)pdm09 subtype' is leading Approximately 97% of viruses detected in the early stages of this season's outbreak (about 85.7% in Tokyo) are the 'A(H1N1)pdm09 subtype'. Because the A(H3N2) Hong Kong type and B type were dominant in the previous season, it is believed that the overall societal herd immunity against A(H1N1) had decreased, triggering this season's ultra-early outbreak. What is the concerning mutant strain 'Subclade K (lineage name: J.2.4.1)'? The primary culprit that has spread rapidly worldwide since the last season (2025–2026) and caused early and major influenza outbreaks is the A(H3N2) Hong Kong mutant strain, 'Subclade K (lineage name: J.2.4.1)'. Antigenic variation and 'glycan shield': Approximately 7 mutations (such as S144N) have accumulated in the protein (HA) on the virus surface. This forms a 'glycan shield' where new glycans (candy-like structures) attach to the top of the virus, acquiring the property of making it difficult for human neutralizing antibodies to bind (immune escape) Impact on the outbreak: Because it has become easier to slip past conventional immunity and the previous season's vaccine strains, it has brought about an outbreak expansion more than a month earlier than usual in countries around the world. Outlook for this season: Currently, A(H1N1) is leading, but there is concern that this 'Subclade K' could spread as a second wave toward the full-scale winter season. 💡 The key to prevention! 'Latest situation on the 2026/27 season vaccine' This season's vaccine has 'all 3 manufacturing strains completely renewed' To respond to major mutations on the virus side (such as the rise of Subclade K), the vaccine (trivalent) for this season decided by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare has had all 3 manufacturing strains renewed from the previous season. A(H1N1)pdm09: A/Switzerland/6849/2025 A(H3N2) Hong Kong type: A/Michigan/105/2025 (strain corresponding to the mutant 'Subclade K') B (Victoria lineage): B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 Note: Since the B-type Yamagata lineage has not been detected anywhere in the world since March 2020, it has been removed, and it is being supplied as a 'trivalent vaccine' again this season. New vaccine options attracting attention Painless spray-type 'Nasal live attenuated influenza vaccine (FluMist® Nasal Spray)' Target: 2 years old to under 19 years old (completed with 1 dose). Features: Induces immunity directly in the nasal mucosa. In a study targeting children for the 2025/26 season, a high effectiveness was shown with an adjusted vaccine effectiveness (VE) against type A of 81%. High-dose inactivated vaccine for seniors (Fluzone High-Dose® intramuscular injection) Target: Although it was developed with a high antigen content for those aged 60 and over, its release and introduction into the routine vaccination program have been postponed for the 2026/27 season due to domestic manufacturing and supply circumstances. Next-generation 'mRNA vaccines' and 'combination vaccines' Development is also rapidly progressing for mRNA influenza vaccines (approved by the US FDA in August 2026 for those aged 50 and over), which can quickly respond to variant strains, as well as combination vaccines that allow for simultaneous vaccination against COVID-19 in a single shot. Summary The early outbreak in Okinawa is occurring due to the combination of "indoor confinement and dryness caused by air conditioning" and "active human movement from both within and outside the country." Furthermore, the virus itself is continuing to mutate, as seen with 'Subclade K', in an attempt to evade immunity. However, this season's vaccines have been updated to strains that are well-equipped to handle these latest variants. Be sure to ventilate frequently even in air-conditioned rooms, and take thorough preventive measures through hand washing and early vaccination. supplementary_news.content: Get AppApp National Are you eligible for a free flu jab? New strain of virus triggers winter warnings A pharmacist is urging people to check their eligibility for a free flu jab as the UK braces for the K-strain flu this winter By Russell Taylerson-Whyte •30 September 2026 JAB TIME: As winter approaches vulnerable groups are being urged to check if they can have a flu vaccination (Image: Getty) A pharmacist is urging people to verify their eligibility for a free NHS flu vaccination as medical experts prepare for the K-strain virus this winter. Concerns over a potentially severe British flu season are growing following a major outbreak currently affecting New Zealand. Subclade K is an offshoot of Influenza A(H3N2) that spreads rapidly through human populations owing to minor genetic mutations. These specific drift alterations mean that older vaccine preparations provide less protection against infection from this particular variant. Strains of H3N2 typically cause more severe illness in older adults and other vulnerable groups than H1N1 or Influenza B variants. These elevated health risks remain a defining feature of the subclade K virus. MORE HEALTH NEWS Brain tumour breakthrough slashes wait to HOURS - and could stop cancer coming back How you might be overdosing on vitamins without even realising Public health professor Michael Baker warns that New Zealand faces historically high mortality rates alongside a sharp rise in hospital admissions. A surge in cases led Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora) to issue public warnings about steep increases in community sickness and clinic visits, reports Neil Shaw for Devon Live. The virus causes symptoms including chills, fever, and severe headaches, prompting New Zealand health leaders to extend free vaccinations to children aged six months to five years. British medical experts routinely analyse southern-hemisphere winter data to predict what the UK might experience later on. Well Pharmacy Deputy Superintendent Wendy Lee is calling on eligible people to secure their vaccinations well before the arrival of cold weather. She said: "The crisis in New Zealand should be a wake-up call to us all, particularly parents of young children, the old and vulnerable. "Flu can come on very quickly, so now is the time to think about protection rather than waiting until cases are already rising. Don't be fooled into thinking that the winter is going to be any less harsh because of the enduring heatwaves during this long summer." Who can get a free flu jab? The official NHS flu vaccination schedule is already rolling out across the country. Starting September 1, children aged two and three, alongside primary and secondary pupils, became eligible for free NHS vaccinations in England and Wales. Pregnant women have also been able to access the vaccine since September 1, while most other qualifying groups become eligible from October 1. These qualifying groups include: Adults aged 65 and over People aged 18 to 64 in clinical risk groups Pregnant women Children born between September 1, 2022 and August 31, 2024, or those in school from Reception through to Year 11 People living in long-stay residential care homes Carers Other groups specified under the national flu vaccination programme. Lee said: "If you're eligible for a free NHS jab, you should check how and where you can get vaccinated, rather than waiting for flu levels to rise." For people who do not meet the free NHS criteria, many pharmacies provide paid-for flu vaccinations. "Flu can be confused with a bad cold because some of the symptoms overlap. But one of the biggest differences is how quickly symptoms appear," Lee said. According to the NHS, flu symptoms can develop very rapidly and can include: Aching body Chills Dry cough Headache High temperature Loss of appetite Runny or blocked nose Sore throat Tiredness Some people can also experience nausea or diarrhoea. Flu is highly contagious and can affect the nose, throat and lungs. While encouraging all those eligible to receive their flu jabs, Wendy urges people not to become overly alarmed. She said: "The evidence so far suggests K is not necessarily more severe than other flu strains in an individual person. The reason it is causing such a big impact appears to be how easily it is spreading and the sheer number of people being infected. "Remember, it takes about two weeks after a flu vaccination for your body to develop antibodies and reach its expected level of protection. The NHS warns the flu vaccine usually takes up to 14 days to work. This means you are not protected, you can still catch flu during those first two weeks if you're exposed before your immune response has developed," Lee advised. supplementary_news.content: C24-UR C41 C42 UK44 Rohi SUBMIT BLOG/ VLOG Latest Pakistan World South Asia China Middle East Entertainment Stocks & Gold Sports Prayers Timings More Opinion Oddities Travel Science & Tech Lifestyle Health Education Crime Environment latest Govt removes Dr Muhammad Salman as PIMS Executive Director Pro-govt forces besieging Yemen's Mocha but yet to recapture it: military sources KP Assembly speaker urges PM Shehbaz to implement peace jirga recommendations Pakistan reports sixth polio case of year from KP Petrol price raised by 88 paisas, diesel cut by Rs1.88 per litre Govt removes Dr Muhammad Salman as PIMS Executive Director Pro-govt forces besieging Yemen's Mocha but yet to recapture it: military sources Influenza Vaccine: A Small Injection That Can Prevent a Serious Illness Flu is not always “just a flu” — vaccination can protect the lungs, the vulnerable and the wider community Published: 11:42 AM, 30 Sep, 2026 Opinion Listen to this article Play Pause Speed: 1.0x Volume: 100% Dr Farzand Ali Every year, particularly when respiratory infections increase, many people develop fever, cough, sore throat, body aches and profound weakness. Most recover within a few days, and because of this, influenza is often dismissed as “just flu.” But influenza deserves greater attention. For some people, influenza can progress to pneumonia, severe respiratory illness, hospitalization and even death. It can also aggravate pre-existing diseases such as asthma, COPD, heart disease and diabetes. The good news is that we have an effective preventive tool: the influenza vaccine. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), seasonal influenza causes approximately one billion infections every year worldwide, including millions of cases of severe illness and hundreds of thousands of respiratory deaths. What exactly is influenza? Influenza is an acute respiratory infection caused mainly by influenza A and B viruses. It spreads easily from person to person through respiratory particles and contaminated hands and surfaces. Typical symptoms include: - Sudden fever - Dry cough - Sore throat - Headache - Muscle and joint pains - Marked tiredness - Runny nose Most healthy people recover without major complications. However, the disease can become much more serious in people with underlying medical problems and other high-risk groups. What is the influenza vaccine? The influenza vaccine is designed to protect against influenza viruses expected to circulate during a particular season. Because influenza viruses continuously evolve, WHO reviews global influenza viruses and recommends updates to vaccine composition twice each year for the Northern and Southern Hemisphere seasons. Most injectable seasonal influenza vaccines are inactivated vaccines and cannot cause influenza infection. Protection develops gradually, and it can take approximately two weeks for the body to develop protective antibodies. Why is influenza vaccination important? The purpose of vaccination is not merely to prevent a few days of fever and cough. Influenza can cause or worsen: - Pneumonia - Severe respiratory illness - Asthma exacerbations - COPD exacerbations - Cardiovascular complications - Hospitalization - Respiratory failure - Death in vulnerable individuals For patients with chronic respiratory diseases, prevention is particularly important. A patient with COPD or severe asthma may be relatively stable, but an influenza infection can precipitate an acute exacerbation requiring emergency treatment or hospitalization. Who should receive the influenza vaccine? WHO particularly identifies the following groups as being at increased risk: 1. Pregnant women Influenza can be more serious during pregnancy. Vaccination is recommended during any stage of pregnancy. 2. Young children Children under 5 years of age, particularly younger children, are at increased risk of complications. 3. Older adults People aged 65 years and above have a higher risk of severe influenza and complications. 4. Patients with chronic diseases Annual vaccination is particularly important for people with: - Asthma - COPD - Chronic lung diseases - Heart disease - Diabetes - Chronic kidney disease - Chronic liver disease - Certain neurological conditions - Other significant chronic medical conditions 5. Immunocompromised individuals Patients with weakened immunity, including those receiving certain cancer treatments or immunosuppressive medicines, may be at increased risk of severe influenza. 6. Healthcare workers Doctors, nurses, paramedics and other healthcare workers have increased exposure to respiratory infections and may transmit influenza to vulnerable patients. Can the influenza vaccine cause influenza? No. The injectable inactivated influenza vaccine cannot cause influenza. Some people may experience mild soreness at the injection site, tiredness, headache, muscle aches or a low-grade fever. These reactions are generally short-lived. Serious allergic reactions are very rare. When should I get vaccinated? Ideally, influenza vaccination should be given before the influenza season begins, allowing approximately two weeks for immunity to develop. However, vaccination may still provide benefit when given later during the influenza season. In tropical and subtropical regions, influenza may circulate throughout the year, with periods of increased activity. Therefore, in Pakistan, vaccination timing should consider local influenza activity, seasonal patterns and availability of the current-season vaccine. How much does the influenza vaccine cost in Pakistan? The price varies according to the manufacturer, formulation, pharmacy and availability. For example, the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) lists Vaxigrip Trivalent influenza vaccine, 0.5 mL, at a registered price of Rs. 1,293.24 per dose in its July 2026 price listing. Actual retail prices may differ, so patients should confirm the current price before purchasing. The vaccine should be obtained from a reputable licensed healthcare provider or pharmacy, and appropriate cold-chain storage must be maintained. Where can people get the vaccine in Pakistan? Depending on current availability, influenza vaccination may be obtained through: - Major hospitals - Vaccination centres - Licensed pharmacies - Private clinics - Occupational-health programmes - Authorized healthcare providers Patients should ask for the current-season influenza vaccine and check the expiry date and storage conditions. My message to the public As a Pulmonologist and Public Health Consultant, I particularly encourage patients with asthma, COPD and other chronic respiratory diseases not to ignore influenza vaccination. A patient with chronic lung disease already has limited respiratory reserve. A preventable viral infection can sometimes turn a stable condition into a serious medical emergency. Similarly, elderly people, pregnant women, young children, people with diabetes or heart disease, immunocompromised patients and healthcare workers should discuss annual influenza vaccination with their healthcare provider. Vaccination is only one component of prevention. We should also: Improve ventilation. Maintain hand hygiene. Cover coughs and sneezes. Avoid close contact when unwell. Stay home when sick. Seek medical attention promptly when severe symptoms develop. A final word We often spend much more time treating disease than preventing it. Influenza vaccination is a simple preventive intervention, but its importance becomes particularly clear when we consider the people most vulnerable to complications. Do not wait for influenza to become pneumonia before thinking about prevention. If you or someone in your family belongs to a high-risk group, talk to your doctor about annual influenza vaccination. Prevention is better than hospitalization — and protecting vulnerable people is a responsibility we all share. Affiliated with the Department of Health (Primary & Secondary) under the Government of Punjab, Dr Farzand Ali plays a pivotal role in advancing healthcare services in the province. His unwavering contributions to the healthcare sector reflect his passion for medicine and his commitment to serving humanity. His work continues to inspire both his colleagues and the community, making him a respected figure in the medical fraternity of Punjab. Close FDA approves new mRNA vaccine ahead of upcoming flu season. By Michaela Harris Published: Sep. 30, 2026 at 5:06 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google HEALTH MINUTE (CNN) - As the U.S. prepares for the upcoming flu season, Americans have a new tool to protect against severe illness: the nation’s first mRNA-based influenza vaccine. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved mFlusiva for adults ages 50 and older, and it marks the first and only seasonal influenza vaccine utilizing mRNA technology. Officials said that flu activity typically begins ramping up in October, with cases often peaking between December and February. Multiple medical groups emphasized that annual vaccination remains the most effective defense against severe complications and hospitalization. Administered as an injection, mFlusiva functions differently than traditional flu vaccines by delivering instructions directly to the body’s cells. “The new vaccine provides a little bit of the genetic material of the influenza virus that allows our cells to make some of the influenza proteins and allows us to develop an immune response to that,” Kawsar Talaat of the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health said. For older adults, the newly approved shot adds another layer of choice. “However, for people 65 years and older, they have multiple choices of enhanced vaccines, so high dose vaccine, adjuvanted vaccine, and the mRNA vaccine,” Talaat said. Traditional flu vaccines remain widely available across different age groups: Standard-Dose and Cell-Based Shots: Standard-dose injections and egg-free cell-based vaccines are approved for individuals ages 6 months and older. Recombinant Vaccines: An egg-free recombinant shot made without influenza viruses is approved for people ages 9 and older. Nasal Spray (FluMist): Available for healthy individuals ages 2 through 49. Because it contains a weakened live virus, it is not recommended for pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals, or people with certain chronic medical conditions. Copyright 2026 KNOE. Influenza A H1N1 Flu: Persistent Symptoms Should Not Be Ignored, Health Guidance Says Influenza A H1N1 Flu Causes and Symptoms: Influenza A (H1N1) is a seasonal viral infection affecting the respiratory system and, in many otherwise healthy adults, the illness can improve without intensive treatment. The infection can begin with symptoms that resemble other forms of seasonal flu. Fever, cough and sore throat are among the commonly reported signs, while headaches, body aches and pronounced tiredness may also occur. For people with mild symptoms, recovery generally involves plenty of rest, adequate fluid intake and measures aimed at easing discomfort. Most healthy adults recover as the illness runs its course. However, prolonged symptoms warrant medical attention. People who do not notice improvement after around five to six days should speak with a healthcare professional rather than continuing to manage the illness without medical advice. The need for caution is particularly important for certain groups. Young children, older adults and people with existing medical conditions should seek professional guidance if they develop symptoms of H1N1. Those requiring assessment can consult a doctor or go to the nearest government health facility, where their condition can be evaluated and further care advised. Recognising the symptoms early and responding appropriately can help people manage seasonal influenza safely. While many cases remain mild, timely medical advice is important when symptoms persist or affect people at higher risk of complications. (Influenza A H1N1 Flu Causes and Symptoms) Ad

(WIBW) - Stormont Vail is hosting its annual drive-through and walk-in flu shot clinics this fall. Flu shots offered through the Stormont Vail clinics are free at various locations in Topeka, Manhattan and Junction City. supplementary_news.content_title: DPH encourages SC residents to get vaccinated as flu season begins
supplementary_news.content: Danika Young Updated Thu, October 1, 2026 at 10:12 PM UTC 0 COLUMBIA, S.C. (WCBD) - As flu season begins, the South Carolina Department of Public Health (DPH) is encouraging residents take steps to avoid illness, including getting an annual seasonal influenza vaccine. Flu season begins in October and extends through May, typically peaking between December and February, DPH says. DPH says the best protection against the illness is the flu shot and that residents 6 months of age and older who are eligible get vaccinated. "Because it takes about two weeks for your body to develop protection after receiving the flu vaccine, we encourage anyone who hasn`t been vaccinated yet to do so before flu activity increases," said Dr. Abdoulaye Diedhiou, State Epidemiologist. "Getting vaccinated helps prevent illness, reduces the risk of severe complications, and protects the broader community." Each year in South Carolina, an average of 250 people die due to complications from the flu, including four pediatric deaths, DPH says. Vaccinations can be obtained at local pharmacies or healthcare providers and those without insurance and those whose insurance does not cover vaccines may be eligible for no-cost vaccines at DPH clinics. For more information about eligibility, call 1-855-472-3432. In addition to vaccines, other precautions are strongly recommended to prevent spread of illnesses like the flu, including washing hands regularly with soap and water, covering your coughs or sneezes with a tissue or an elbow and staying home and away from others when sick. DPH says it recommends talking with a healthcare provider about what vaccines are right for residents. To find a vaccine provider near you, visit DPHs vaccine finder.
